lead.t: Vibe coding narrowed the gap between people in tech
, so the edge now belongs to whoever can solve the hardest problems solo with AI agents.

paras.t: Even where engineers still lead, the lead got shorter. What was ten years ahead a year ago is perhaps two years ahead now. And the gap closed because of vibe coding. Basically, you build software by telling an AI agent what you want, and that
enables solo building end to end
From the market’s perspective, a year ago
you were worth as much as the complexity of the problems you could see as a product or business person
. But to solve them, you needed a whole team. Now that limit is gone, and you can solve the problem you saw on your own.
So today you are worth as much as the complexity of the problems you can solve.
In turn,
complex problems require a higher mastery of working with LLM agents
. That mastery starts with questions, because any sophisticated software begins with them.
What to ask takes business and product expertise.
How to ask is a second skill.
It means framing the question, decomposing the answer and choosing the next question.
Then at some point you realize that an LLM works on coherence, much as a brain does. It will answer any question with whatever fits best with what it was given, and it follows your framing.
So whoever does not learn to talk to an LLM properly becomes delusional.
The cure is evals and benchmarks
. Evals test your work, and benchmarks test your choice of model.
The next thing you hit is the
context window

. One start of an agent on a task is one run. A run sees only what fits in its context window. A complex problem does not fit one context window. Past a point the window fills with everything the task has touched, and the model gets dumber and starts to hallucinate. That is
context rot
So you split the work into runs, and one agent’s output becomes the next agent’s input. Then you decide what each run sees and what it never sees. That is
context routing
. Runs, handoffs and context routing together make
orchestration
. This is how you solve a problem too big for one context window. However, at some point you understand that
orchestration without evals at each step is a delusion at scale
. Primarily because the error of the first run becomes a fact for every run after it. So you decide to build an eval for each step, and one for the whole chain too.
After a while some steps turn routine and no longer need a model, so you
replace it with code
. Code is cheaper and deterministic (which means it gives the same output every time). Where a step still needs a model, benchmarks tell you which one, or whether to add a second.
But every run still starts from zero, and whatever the system figured out yesterday is gone by the next one. So you give it
memory

that outlives a single context window and is shared between runs. Decisions go there, gotchas, what you tried and what failed. Only what passed an eval goes into memory, and a failure is stored as a failure. Otherwise the system starts remembering its own mistakes as facts.

Up to this point the orchestrator is you. You decide which run goes next, what it sees and where its output goes. Then you write an onboarding protocol, a short file that tells a new agent who it is and how it joins the system. Now
your agents start calling each other instead of you

. One drafts, another pushes back, the first one revises, and it all settles against your evals. A program now picks who wakes up and collects the results, and you step in only for the real decisions.
At some point
the system runs on its own

. You wake up, read what it built overnight, make sure you and your agents learned the gotchas, and set the next batch of tasks. Most of your time now goes into shaping a task the system can deliver by itself. So you are back to asking questions, only now you ask them of the whole system instead of one model. This is sophisticated orchestration, and
it lets one person solve problems that used to take a whole team.

stages.label: Stage I. Solo: you and one run
Stage II. Orchestration: you and a system of runs

ladder.closing: At that point you have stopped renting a model to talk to and started owning the system around it.

rungs.title: Chat
rungs.sub: You ask, it answers. It talks, you act.
rungs.think: It predicts a likely answer, and a likely answer can be wrong.
rungs.skill: You decided to check what ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini says before you use it.
text: You open ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini and type. Behind each chat there is an LLM, a large language model: GPT from OpenAI, Claude from Anthropic, Gemini from Google.
An LLM is a compressed statistical model of language. It predicts the next piece of text, so a wrong answer sounds as sure as a right one.
Most LLM users are here. This is important to understand, because these are the people LLM companies actually build their features for.
tools: ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini, in the browser or on the phone

rungs.title: Agent
rungs.sub: You let it run commands on its own.
rungs.was: AI is something I ask for advice.
rungs.think: AI is something I hand work to.
rungs.skill: You decided to run Claude Code or Codex in a terminal with bypass mode on and let it act.
text: The same models also come as agents that work on your computer. Claude Code runs on Claude, Codex runs on GPT.

You switch on bypass mode, so it stops asking your permission, and let it run commands on its own. This is where your chatbox becomes an agent, because agency means it acts by itself. Every time you start it on a task, that is one run.

Before you let it act, keep the project in git and save a version before every run, so a run that breaks something is undone by going back to that version. Read what it changed before you accept it, and never let it see your passwords and keys.

From here two things grow in parallel. One is its mind: memory, context, judgment. The other is its hands, the tools it can touch: the terminal, files, the web, other services through their APIs, and MCP servers, which are plug-ins that connect it to those services.
Connect it to your calendar through an MCP server, and it books the meeting itself instead of telling you how.
tools: Claude Code, Codex or another vendor’s command-line agent
A terminal with permission to act
Git

rungs.title: Standing instructions
rungs.sub: The file it reads every time.
rungs.was: It remembers what I told it last time.
rungs.think: It knows only what is written down for it.
rungs.skill: You decided to keep a global CLAUDE.md and one per project.
text: You find CLAUDE.md, the instruction file the agent reads every time you start it, but you barely touch it. So it runs on whatever it happened to pick up from talking to you.
Later you learn there are two of them. The global one says who the agent always is, and the project one says what this project needs.
tools: CLAUDE.md for Claude Code
AGENTS.md for Codex

rungs.title: Context rot
rungs.sub: You keep adding to the file and the model gets dumber.
rungs.was: The more I give it, the smarter it gets.
rungs.think: Past a point, more context makes it dumber.
rungs.skill: You decided to keep CLAUDE.md under 200 lines and move the rest into documents it opens when needed.
text: The context window is everything the model sees at once. Whatever is outside it does not exist for the model.
You keep adding to CLAUDE.md, the task pulls in more and more files, and at some point the window gets so full that the model gets dumber and starts making things up. That is context rot.

An agent is only as honest as its context, so you learn to keep the file tight, global and project files together under about 200 lines. Everything else goes into documents the agent opens only when it needs them.

rungs.title: The question
rungs.sub: One goal per request, with everything that goal needs.
rungs.was: A bad answer means a weak model.
rungs.think: A bad answer usually means a bad question.
rungs.skill: You decided to put one goal in each request and say what the answer must contain.
text: You stop throwing a wish into the box and start framing the question. You say what exactly you want and what the answer must contain, and after reading the answer you choose the next question.

An LLM works with meaning the way a person does, so how you frame the question changes the answer you get. It also follows your framing, so a leading question gets you agreement. Whoever talks to it badly becomes delusional.

rungs.title: Evals
rungs.sub: You stop guessing and start measuring.
rungs.was: It looks right, so it works.
rungs.think: Nothing works until a test says so.
rungs.skill: You decided to write tests and bring in a Judge agent that checks the first one.
text: You write evals, small tests that prove the result still works. Before the run starts, you write down what done means.
Almost everyone skips this step, and this is where you start measuring instead of hoping.
Here you also bring in a Judge agent, a second model whose job is to check the first one. It can be your QA agent, or in my case, The Order. The idea is to automate your evaluation.
tools: The test runners you already use
A Judge agent
Scripts that read the output and say pass or fail

rungs.title: Benchmarks
rungs.sub: The same task on another model, another vendor.
rungs.think: The best model for my task changes every few months.
rungs.skill: You decided to write a script that sends the same task to several vendors and scores each with your evals.
text: You run your own task on models from different vendors and compare speed, cost and how often the eval passes. Which model is good at what changes every few months, so you keep track.
Picking the wrong model can be a costly mistake, and from inside one chat you will never see it.
tools: A subscription or an API key per vendor
One script that sends the same prompt to each
Your evals from LVL 5 as the score

rungs.title: Decomposition
rungs.sub: One context window runs out, so you split the work into several runs.
rungs.was: One smart agent can do the whole thing.
rungs.think: A big problem is a chain of small runs.
rungs.skill: You decided to start subagents and pass files from one run to the next.
text: The task no longer fits into one context window, so you cut it into subtasks. Each subtask gets its own run with a fresh context window, and one agent’s output becomes the next agent’s input.
You feel the cost right away: handoffs between agents, and drift away from the goal. Over time you learn to split only when the work does not fit one context window.
tools: Subagents, which are agents your agent starts for one piece of the work
Task queues
Plain files passed from one run to the next

rungs.title: Context routing
rungs.sub: Who gets which part of the context, and who never sees it.
rungs.was: Give every agent everything, just in case.
rungs.think: What a run does not see cannot mislead it.
rungs.skill: You decided to keep a list per step of what the run receives and where it may write.
text: Each run gets what its step needs: the task description, the previous output, the files it must read. It does not get anything that could bias it.
Up to LVL 11 you are the one who decides this for every step, so the orchestrator is you. At LVL 12 a program takes over that role.
tools: A list per step of what the run receives
Inputs it can read but not change
A rule for what a run may write and where

rungs.title: Evals at every step
rungs.sub: And one on the whole chain.
rungs.was: I check the result at the end.
rungs.think: Every step needs its own check, or the first mistake spreads through the chain.
rungs.skill: You decided to put an eval between runs, so a failed step passes nothing on.
text: A mistake in the first run becomes a fact for every run after it. So each step gets its own eval, and the whole chain gets one too.
Orchestration without evals at each step is a delusion at scale. A step that fails its eval does not pass its output on.
tools: The same evals from LVL 5, now placed between runs

rungs.title: Code over model
rungs.sub: You tear down half of what you built.
rungs.was: More AI makes the system better.
rungs.think: Wherever a step is predictable, code does it better than a model.
rungs.skill: You decided to turn routine steps into ordinary functions and hooks that check the output.
text: At some point you tear down half of what you built to make it leaner. Every step that became routine turns into code.
Code is cheaper and gives the same output every time, and you test it like any other function. The model stays only where there is real uncertainty.
A lean core is easier to manage and, importantly, to trust.
tools: Ordinary functions
Schedulers
Validation scripts
Hooks that check the agent’s output before it lands

rungs.title: Memory
rungs.sub: What survives a session and is shared between runs.
rungs.was: Each session is a fresh start.
rungs.think: What the system learned has to outlive the session, if it passed an eval.
rungs.skill: You decided to give each agent a memory file and every run a shared store to search.
text: You find MEMORY.md, memory that outlives one context window and is shared between agents. Decisions go there, gotchas, what you tried and what failed.
Only what passed an eval goes into memory, and a failure is stored as a failure. Work accumulates, and smart-in-the-moment turns into smart-over-time.
tools: A memory file per agent
A shared store every run can search
Full-text search over past sessions

rungs.title: Agents call each other
rungs.sub: An orchestrator picks who wakes, hands off, collects.
rungs.was: I have to drive every step myself.
rungs.think: My job is the decisions, and the agents handle the handoffs.
rungs.skill: You decided to write an onboarding protocol and a message format your agents share.
text: You write an onboarding protocol that tells a new agent who it is and how it joins. Now your agents call each other instead of you.
One drafts, the Judge pushes back, the first one revises, and it all settles against your evals. You step in only for the real decisions.
tools: A list of agents and how to reach each
A message format they all use
An orchestrator with a cap on how many times a task can bounce between agents

rungs.title: Autonomy
rungs.sub: Your agents run on their own.
rungs.was: My work is doing the task.
rungs.think: My work is shaping tasks the system can deliver without me.
rungs.skill: You decided to set up schedules and watchers, so the system runs overnight and leaves logs.
text: Your daily routine is to wake up and see what they built during the night. You make sure you and your agents learned the gotchas. Then you build the next batch of tasks.
Most of your own time goes into shaping a task that fits your system, so it delivers by itself.
Without you, no agent spends money, deletes anything or publishes anything.
tools: Schedules
Watchers that alert you
Logs, so every mechanism leaves a trail you can read in the morning

rungs.title: Departments
rungs.sub: Teams of agents, each with its own discipline.
rungs.was: I run a set of agents.
rungs.think: I run something closer to a company.
rungs.skill: You decided to group your agents into departments, each with its own Judge, and let a product manager agent run whole projects through them.
text: Highly speculative, I’m not here yet.
You build departments of agents: marketing, business development, engineering with devs and QAs. Each has its own Judge and follows the protocol, and all of them know about each other.
Next you bring in a product manager agent that builds whole projects overnight using your departments. Nobody has shipped this yet.
